claims.text: The initial Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles are equiatomic, sub-10 nm, disordered solid solutions.
The initial nanoparticles have high surface energy.
The sluggish-diffusion assumption breaks down for Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt particles below 15 nm.
Below 15 nm, surface-to-volume effects dominate structural evolution.
Surface-to-volume effects drive rapid segregation and Ostwald ripening during heating to 1000 K.
Surface diffusion and surface-segregation energy gradients dominate over bulk lattice-diffusion barriers in sub-10 nm particles.
The high surface-to-volume ratio lowers the activation energy for surface diffusion.
Enhanced surface diffusion allows rapid elemental segregation in Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles.
Au and Cu have sufficiently lower surface energies to segregate to the nanoparticle surface.
Pt and Co become enriched in the particle core or form Pt/Co-rich precipitates or segregation layers.
Trace oxygen may cause surface oxides or compounds to form.
Surface-mediated transport bypasses the bulk sluggish-diffusion barrier.
The smallest particles dissolve by Ostwald ripening to reduce total surface energy.
Particles smaller than 5 nm will be rapidly lost during annealing.
Annealing will produce significant shape evolution toward faceted or core-shell morphologies.
The annealed nanoparticles will not retain a stable single-phase solid solution.
High-entropy-alloy theory associates high mixing entropy and sluggish diffusion with retention of a disordered solid-solution state.
The sluggish-diffusion hypothesis for high-entropy alloys is not well supported experimentally.
For particles larger than 50 nm, bulk sluggish diffusion may dominate and preserve the entropy-stabilized state for longer times.
The critical size and the balance between surface and bulk diffusion depend on constituent surface energies, impurities, and temperature.

contradictions.description: The mechanism describes dissolution of the smallest particles by Ostwald ripening, which normally increases the surviving mean particle size, whereas the supporting branch of the falsification rule calls for 'rapid size reduction.' Loss of small particles and reduction of overall particle size are not equivalent outcomes.
